Beállítom Az augusztus 20-i magyarországi nemzeti ünnep alkalmából levelet írt Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök Magyar Péternek. A budapesti ukrán nagykövetség Facebook-oldalán közzétett levél szerint Zelenszkij „a legközelebbi megfelelő időpontra” meghívta Kijevbe a magyar miniszterelnököt. A levélben Zelenszkij gratulált a magyar népnek Szent István napjához, és megköszönte, hogy Magyarország következetesen támogatja Ukrajna szuverenitását és területi integritását. Elmondása szerint különösen nagyra értékelik a magyarok humanitárius segítségnyújtását, és főleg az ukrán gyerekek és katonák rehabilitációjának támogatását. Zelenszkij a levélben megerősítette, hogy kész nyílt és konstruktív együttműködést folytatni az ukrán-magyar kapcsolatok további erősítésére „és a teljes körű együttműködés fejlesztése érdekében, közös európai jövőnkért.” Augusztus 20-ára virradóra, illetve napközben egy második körben Oroszország ballisztikus rakétákkal és drónokkal támadta Kijevet és a város környékét. A támadásokban legalább 17 ember meghalt és több mint 40 megsebesült. Zelenszkij meghívásával kapcsolatban kerestük a Miniszterelnökséget, amennyiben érdemben válaszolnak, beszámolunk róla. One new shelter, designed to accommodate more than 1,000 children, is being built in Samar district ahead of the new academic year. by Kyiv Post | Aug. 27, 2026, 8:28 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Children wait before evacuation from the city of Sloviansk to the city of Dnipro, on July 6, 2022. (Photo by MIGUEL MEDINA / AFP) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip The network of shelters is being expanded in the Dnipropetrovsk region as local authorities prepare for the upcoming academic year. In Samar district, a new underground school shelter is being built, designed to accommodate more than 1,000 children. Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Military Administration said Thursday, Aug. 27, that he had begun inspections of schools across the region, assessing their readiness for the beginning of classes on Sept. 1. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “We are expanding the network of shelters so that boys and girls can attend their regular classrooms,” Hanzha said, explaining that the new underground shelter will have a capacity five times greater than that of the existing one. “It will also have enough space for students from a neighboring gymnasium,” he continued. Advertisement Schools ready for the new academic year In Samar district, 63 schools are expected to operate either in person or in a hybrid format, while students at 10 other institutions will study remotely. Hanzha said the schools are generally ready to begin classes, although several outstanding issues still require attention, particularly children’s meals, schools’ energy resilience, “and, above all,” Hanzha said, “the safety of the learning process.” Local officials were instructed to resolve the issues as quickly as possible. During the inspections, Hanzha also visited other schools in the district. Other Topics of Interest Russian Epicentr Strike in Kharkiv Kills 1, Injures 5 Firefighters extinguished a 300-square-meter blaze after a Russian jet-powered drone struck the hypermarket. One school received Hr. 4 million (approximately $89,855) from the regional budget to improve its energy efficiency. Local authorities also discussed the government’s “School Starter Pack” program, under which families of children entering first grade can receive Hr. 5,000 (approximately $112.32) for essential school supplies. Czech-funded school shelter opened in Nikopol On July 1, Hanzha and the Extraordinary and Plenipotentiary Ambassador of the Czech Republic to Ukraine, Luboš Veselý, opened a newly built shelter at a lyceum in the frontline community of Nikopol on July 1. Advertisement Before the shelter’s completion, students at the lyceum had to rely on remote learning, as the school previously lacked adequate protection during air raids and possible strikes. Although the digitalization of education during the war has helped thousands of Ukrainian schoolchildren overcome learning loss, authorities are searching for ways to bring more children back to in-person classes so they do not miss out on direct contact with teachers and classmates, as well as the general school experience. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/23/fami.text: Relatives of people who died after buying lethal substances from Canadian poison seller Kenneth Law are due to speak in court this week, as a judge begins deliberating how long the former chef should spend in prison.Justice Michelle Fuerst has set aside four days at a court in Newmarket, just north of Toronto, to hear victim impact statements and further evidence. It is not yet clear when she will hand down her sentence.Law pleaded guilty in May to aiding the suicides of 14 people in Canada. Prosecutors dropped murder charges after concluding they did not have enough evidence to secure a conviction over the online forums where he advised people on how to end their lives.Under an agreed statement of facts signed by both sides, Law admitted seeking out buyers by posting on a suicide discussion forum under a false name and offering lethal products for sale. His packages reached customers in at least 41 countries, including China, France and Brazil, with 330 sent to the United Kingdom.Several bereaved families have said they are angry Law will not stand trial for murder, arguing he bears direct responsibility for the deaths of mostly young and vulnerable people. Legal experts say prosecutors are likely to push for a heavy sentence, potentially up to 20 years.UK deaths under scrutiny since 2023Britain's role in the case came to light soon after Law's arrest. In August 2023, UK authorities were investigating 88 deaths linked to Law, with the National Crime Agency working to trace people in Britain who may have bought his products.Police in Surrey had contacted Law in October 2022 over the death of 22-year-old Tom Parfett, who died in 2021 after apparently visiting one of Law's websites, and a later inquiry into his death raised questions about why the force had not investigated Law further.'Not a diabolical madman'Earlier this month, Canada's Globe and Mail reported details of interviews Law gave to a psychiatrist in prison after his guilty plea. According to court documents obtained by the paper, Law said he had been "trying to serve a need that I thought was humane," adding: "I'm not a diabolical madman."The documents show that after his arrest in 2023, Law considered himself blameless, insisting he never made the final decision to end anyone's life and was simply selling a product, the Globe reported.Law, now in his 60s, worked as a chef at a luxury hotel in downtown Toronto before setting up his online forums during the Covid-19 pandemic. He has admitted to shipping lethal substances within Canada and abroad, typically charging around $80 per package.Among his victims was 18-year-old Jeshennia Bedoya-Lopez, who died in 2022. Speaking outside court in May, her father Leonardo Bedoya said he had found her dead in her bedroom. Describing his only daughter as the "light in my life", he called the prosecutors' decision to drop the murder charges "a disgrace."

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/o.text: Packages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters View image in fullscreen Packages of perished goods piled outside an Intermarché store in Paris the day after a cyber-attack targeted refrigeration and freezer systems. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters France Not cool: who hacked France’s supermarket fridges? Whether it was youngsters proving their skills or state sabotage, Europe’s most hacked country was left with a mountain of waste after food began cooking in freezers Kim Willsher in Paris Sat 17 Oct 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Shortly before midnight last Sunday, the digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise. In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber-attack, hackers had remotely overridden the temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets pushing them from as low as -27C (-16.6F) to well over 50C (122F). Over the next four to six hours, the food inside first defrosted, then slowly began to cook. Shop staff arriving early to restock shelves reported catching a blast of hot air, like opening an oven, when they went to fill freezers. One Normandy supermarket reported a number of its freezers had been pushed to 80C (176F). In certain stores, the extreme temperature rise had sparked fires triggering sprinklers and water damage. “It was a catastrophe,” said one worker at the large Intermarché supermarket in the south-west suburb of Issy-les-Moulineaux in Paris . “They pushed the freezers here up to 62C. Everything had to be thrown away. It was such a waste.” View image in fullscreen Supermarket staff had to remove tons of spoiled food and work late to reorder and restock shelves. Photograph: Lucien Libert/Reuters After removing tons of spoiled food, staff at the store worked until almost midnight on Monday to reorder and restock shelves. “Thankfully, we were able to get things almost back to normal the same day,” another shop worker added. “But we had to clear out everything in the freezers.” If shop managers first assumed it was an isolated failure, it soon became clear up to 700 stores – including those from the Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains along with a number of smaller independent shops – had been victims of a cyber-attack. Dominique Schelcher, the president of Coopérative U, said 80 of its 2,000 supermarkets had been targeted. “This is a completely unprecedented, unexpected, and extremely serious attack. In my entire professional career, I’ve never seen anything like it,” the shocked executive told French radio. The Paris public prosecutor’s office immediately opened an investigation into the latest in a series of cyber-attacks that have made France the most hacked country in Europe . Gérôme Billois , a partner in the cybersecurity and technology company Wavestone, said the hack had the hallmarks of political sabotage. “The two most feasible scenarios are either it was a group of youngsters or activists who wanted to blow up a few freezers to prove what they could do, or it was a destabilising attack, what we call sabotage, by internal or external state actors,” he said. View image in fullscreen A woman walks past empty refrigerators at an Intermarché supermarket in Névez, western France. Photograph: Fred Tanneau/AFP/Getty “As for the attack’s signature, the most likely scenario is still a destabilisation attack – one designed to convey the message to populations that they are not safe, to convey the impression that the government is falling apart, and ultimately to instil fear. “Currently there are two international actors known for doing this sort of thing: Iran and Russia.” The hackers had pirated the controllers supplied by the Danish company Danfoss that controls the freezers and fridges. Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. Initial investigations suggest the hackers disabled alarm systems before tampering with the thermostats, or extended the defrost programme by several hours to avoid triggering alarms. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” that customers install updates or replace obsolete unsupported systems. The affected refrigeration units were “running outdated firmware”, it said. In the days following the first wave of attacks, France’s cyber-attack alert centre ANSSI confirmed supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted. Marta Rybczyńska, a cybersecurity specialist and researcher, said she had found previous security warnings about old supermarket freezers running out-of-date software and newer models not having firmware updated. 1:05 French supermarket director apologises after cyber-attack spoils fresh and frozen food - video “Some of these freezers hadn’t been supported by the manufacturers for several years and there were notices saying they should be replaced. Other freezers were newer but the software hadn’t been updated,” Rybczyńska said. “The hackers found these weaknesses and used them.” She added: “Many of the freezers appear to have been running with a default password. The hackers were able to modify or turn off the alerts so the shops only realised when the first person arrived in the morning and saw the damage that had been done.” The most recent French cyber-attack mirrors a similar incident in the US in August when connected fridges and freezers at a dozen military commissaries – on-base food stores – went into unscheduled defrost cycles overnight causing massive food loss. France is the most heavily pirated country in Europe by the volume of records exposed by hackers, according to the cybersecurity and risk management company Upguard. In the last three years, hackers have breached France’s health system, France Travail, the government-run jobseekers agency, the National Agency for Identity Documents (ANTS) and most of the big mobile phone companies. This summer, the economy and finance ministry lost the personal and fiscal records of 678,000 taxpayers to a series of cyber-attacks. View image in fullscreen Supermarket employees restock goods in Nancy, north-east France. Photograph: Muhammed Said Tako/Anadolu/Getty Billois says France has fallen behind in addressing cybersecurity and has still not adopted the EU’s Cyber Resilience Act (2024) that introduced mandatory security for internet-connected devices. “It’s a text that’s not political and that everyone agrees on but is delayed because there’s always more urgent legislation or there are quibbles about amendments, and this has been a disaster,” he said. In the UK, the cyber security and resilience (network and information systems) bill to tackle cyber threats, is wending a similarly tortuous way through parliament. However, it fails to directly cover the food industry. Supermarket boss Schelcher was quick to shift the blame for the attack on to unnamed refrigeration contractors who maintain the cold aisle equipment. “Our supermarkets are not customers of Danfoss,” he told RTL radio. As yet, no individual or group has claimed responsibility for the supermarket cyber-attack; Paris prosecutors have instructed detectives from its anti-cybercrime unit but Billois says finding the hackers will take time. “It’s possible they’ll be identified eventually, but it could take weeks if not months to be certain because hackers know how to hide their tracks,” Billois said. The Guardian view on food security: we have just-in-time, we need just-in-case | Editorial Read more Rybczyńska added: “Whether it’s possible to trace the hackers depends on their level of capability; if it’s a handful of youngsters, it’s easier because they probably won’t have thought to remove traces. If they are professionals it’s more complicated and will take longer. If they’re in a foreign country, it’ll be extremely difficult.” The total cost of the cyber-attack has yet to be calculated but Thierry Cotillard, the CEO of Intermarché, said losses could run to “tens of millions of euros”, which store companies say is unlikely to be covered by their insurance. “It’s a bizarre story,” Billois added. “There’s a shared responsibility between the supermarkets, the refrigeration companies who are sub-contractors and who maintain the material, and the software company. We cannot say who is to blame except, of course, the hackers. “But in the end it comes down to freezers connected to the internet without being adequately secured.
